'Mridul won't dance, he's the shy one,' Tauji announced to the whole courtyard, and everyone laughed kindly.
Mridul smiled and stayed on the stairs. Later Darshan sat beside him with two plates of jalebi.
'You didn't say anything when he said that.'
'What's there to say? It's true. I'm the shy one. Since I was six.'
'You ran the college quiz last month. In front of three hundred people.'
'That's different. That was a mic and a script.'
'You also argued with the auto driver in Marathi for twenty minutes this morning and won.'
Mridul laughed. 'That's different too.'
'Everything's different when it doesn't fit the label, na?'
Mridul looked at the dancers. 'Maybe I stay on the stairs because they expect me on the stairs.'
Darshan held out a hand. 'One song. I'll be terrible next to you.'

qa.q: How many people did Mridul run the college quiz in front of?
qa.a: Mridul ran it in front of three hundred people.

qa.q: Why does Mridul say 'It's true. I'm the shy one'?
qa.a: Mridul has heard the label since age six, so it feels like a fact about who he is, and anything that doesn't fit gets filed away as 'different'.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that began to shift the label?
qa.a: Darshan named specific times Mridul was bold, the quiz and the auto driver, then offered a low-pressure step, one song together, so Mridul could act outside the label.

qa.q: How might Tauji see Mridul if he joins the dancing?
qa.a: Tauji may be surprised and start to see more than 'the shy one', since the label came from habit rather than a fresh look at who Mridul is now.

grounding: Shows a young man long called 'the shy one' by family who acts to fit it, and a cousin who sees more and helps him step out.

subtype: Being labelled by peers or family [Receiver]
passage: In our family, my brother was 'the doctor' and I was 'the one who failed'. I flunked Class 12 physics once, at seventeen, and after that the words came up at every function. 'Devika? She's still figuring things out.' I started believing it. I stopped applying for things. Why fill a form when everyone knew how it ended? Then, in the year I was repeating, Manjula Aunty from the flat downstairs asked me to help with her tailoring accounts. I found a mistake of eleven hundred rupees in her books. She looked at me over her glasses and said, 'You're sharp with numbers. Did you know that?' Nobody had said a sentence like that to me in a year. It's a small thing. But I applied for B.Com that month, and I'm in my final year now.

qa.q: How big was the mistake Devika found in Manjula Aunty's books?
qa.a: It was a mistake of eleven hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why did Devika stop applying for things?
qa.a: Hearing 'the one who failed' at every function made Devika believe it, so every form seemed to have a known ending and trying felt pointless.

qa.q: What made Manjula Aunty's sentence so powerful?
qa.a: It named a specific strength Devika had just shown, being sharp with numbers, which gave her a new picture of herself that was strong enough to act on.

qa.q: How might Devika's family see the B.Com application?
qa.a: The family might be surprised, since they had stopped expecting much, and it could start to loosen the label they had been repeating.

grounding: Shows a young woman called the failure of the family who begins to live the label, until one neighbour notices a real strength.

Coach's notes, district youth football camp, Day 9
Asif (19, midfield). The squad has called him 'Silent Asif' since day one, and I've noticed he has started living up to it. He doesn't call for the ball even when he's free. In the huddle he stands at the back. Today, in a small-sided game, he made a pass that split the defence, and when I asked him how he saw it, he explained the whole move clearly, pointing at the cones. That's not a silent player. That's a player nobody has asked. I told the group what I'd seen, and I've asked Asif to lead the warm-up drill tomorrow. He looked alarmed, then nodded. I'll keep the drill short and stand nearby. I'll also ask the squad to drop the nickname.
Karthik

qa.q: What has the squad called Asif since day one?
qa.a: The squad has called him 'Silent Asif'.

qa.q: Why might Asif have stopped calling for the ball?
qa.a: Asif may have felt self-conscious after hearing 'Silent Asif' again and again, starting to see himself that way, so speaking up on the pitch felt out of character.

qa.q: Which of Karthik's steps is most likely to shift the label, and why?
qa.a: Asking Asif to lead the warm-up gives him a real chance to be seen differently, while keeping it short and standing nearby makes the step manageable.

qa.q: How might Asif's teammates see him after he leads the warm-up?
qa.a: The teammates may start to notice the clear thinker Karthik saw, and the nickname may feel less true once they hear Asif explain a drill.

grounding: Shows a coach's note on a young player labelled 'Silent Asif' who starts to fit the label, and one adult who sees more and gives him a way to show it.

subtype: Being labelled by peers or family [Receiver]
passage:
Wednesday

At Tai's wedding lunch today, Mama said it again, laughing: "Tushar? He's our family's failure. Dropped engineering, now works in a print shop." Everyone laughed. I laughed too.

Funny thing is, I've started acting like it. I don't apply for anything. I don't answer when uncles ask about plans. If I'm the failure, why try? The word sits on me like a shirt I didn't choose.

But this evening at the shop something happened. Ganga-mausi, who owns it, was checking the wedding cards I'd set. She held one up to the light. "Tushar, you fixed the spacing on the Marathi lines without me telling you. You have an eye. Have you thought of learning design properly?"

Nobody has ever said "you have an eye" to me.

I walked home the long way. Maybe "failure" isn't all of it. Maybe I'll look up that design course. Just look.

qa.q: What had Tushar fixed on the wedding cards without being told?
qa.a: The spacing on the Marathi lines.

qa.q: What does Tushar mean when he says the word sits on him "like a shirt I didn't choose"?
qa.a: Tushar feels trapped in a label others put on him; he never agreed to it, but he has started living in it anyway.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Tushar, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Ganga-mausi noticing his eye for design and suggesting a course. One person seeing more than the label gave him a different picture of himself to try.

qa.q: How might Ganga-mausi see Tushar compared with how his family sees him?
qa.a: Ganga-mausi sees a careful worker with real skill, not "the failure". Because she watches his work every day, she notices strengths the family jokes never mention.

grounding: A young man labelled the family failure begins acting like it, until his employer notices his skill and helps shift how he sees himself.
